content: This is an updated version of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2015. Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by recurrent seizures. While most individuals respond to standard antiepileptic drugs, approximately 30% of patients continue to experience seizures despite treatment with multiple antiepileptic medications. Sulthiame, also known as sultiame, is an antiepileptic drug commonly used in Europe and Israel. This review evaluates the evidence for the use of sulthiame as an add-on therapy for epilepsy. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of sulthiame as an add-on therapy for individuals with epilepsy, regardless of the underlying cause, in comparison to placebo or other antiepileptic drugs. For the most recent update, a comprehensive search was conducted in several databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies, MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP Search Portal, up to January 17, 2019. No language restrictions were applied. Additionally, manufacturers of sulthiame and researchers in the field were contacted to identify ongoing or unpublished studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of sulthiame as an add-on therapy, regardless of the level of blinding (single, double, or unblinded), in individuals of any age with epilepsy of any cause. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion and extracted relevant data. The outcomes assessed included: (1) a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency from baseline to the end of follow-up, (2) complete cessation of seizures during follow-up, (3) mean seizure frequency, (4) time-to-treatment withdrawal, (5) adverse effects, and (6) quality of life. Primary analyses were conducted using an intention-to-treat approach, and results were presented as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). However, due to the limited number of trials, the analysis was primarily narrative. Only one placebo-controlled trial met the inclusion criteria. This trial involved 37 infants with newly diagnosed West syndrome and was funded by DESITIN Pharma, Germany. In this study, sulthiame was administered as an add-on therapy to pyridoxine. The trial did not report data for several key outcomes, including a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, mean seizure frequency, or quality of life. For the outcome of complete cessation of seizures during a nine-day follow-up period, the risk ratio for add-on sulthiame compared to placebo was 11.14 (95% CI 0.67 to 184.47), but this result was not statistically significant (P = 0.09). The number of infants experiencing one or more adverse events did not differ significantly between the sulthiame and placebo groups (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.64; P = 0.63). Somnolence was more frequently reported in the sulthiame group compared to placebo, but this difference was also not statistically significant (RR 3.40, 95% CI 0.42 to 27.59; P = 0.25). Due to incomplete data, meaningful analysis of time-to-treatment withdrawal and adverse effects could not be performed. The authors concluded that sulthiame may lead to seizure cessation when used as an add-on therapy to pyridoxine in infants with West syndrome. However, the reliability of this finding is highly uncertain due to the small sample size and significant risk of bias in the included study. The lack of detailed information on blinding and incomplete reporting of outcomes further reduced the certainty of the evidence. No conclusions could be drawn regarding adverse effects, quality of life, or mean reduction in seizure frequency. Additionally, there is no evidence to support the use of sulthiame as an add-on therapy for individuals with epilepsy outside of West syndrome. Large, multi-center randomized controlled trials are necessary to provide robust evidence to guide clinical practice if sulthiame is to be considered as an add-on therapy for epilepsy.
